title: Most pathway-model memories persist over long periods and survive recall

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Most pathway-model memories persist over long periods and survive recall

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In the surveyed ODE pathway models with UCS-based memory, most networks retain the bulk of their memories over waiting periods up to 100 times the initial one, and testing (recalling) a memory generally does not destroy it and in rare cases strengthens it.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Biswas S 2022, Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions › 2. Results › 2.4. Memory Effects Are Stable over Long Periods

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Overall, we conclude that while some networks have a limit on how long they retain training, the majority of networks can retain the bulk of their possible memories over very long time periods and that in general, memory ‘access’ does not destroy the memory but can, in some rare cases, increase memory.

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Biswas S, Clawson W, Levin M, “Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions”, International journal of molecular sciences (2022), doi:10.3390/ijms24010285; section “2. Results › 2.4. Memory Effects Are Stable over Long Periods”. Scope: 30 ODE pathway models from BioModels showing UCS-based memory

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2022-grn-learning-11: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.90

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The waiting periods, recall intervention, and retention outputs are explicit. Reanalysis can resolve the claim for the surveyed models without new empirical data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For the 30 UCS-memory models, measure retained memory after 10- and 100-fold waiting periods with and without intermediate recall. Compare losses and gains against the stated bulk-retention and recall criteria.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Simulation time has model-specific biological meaning.

Only UCS-based memory was tested for this result.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.86
operationalizability: 0.96
data existence: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.86
discriminating power: 0.9

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Persistence and recall are defined as delayed readouts of the same response variable, and a dedicated time-lag script is in the public repository along with the source models. Re-running that assay on the UCS-memory subset confirms or refutes both the long-delay retention claim and the claim about recall. The computation is heavy but specified.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For the models that show UCS-based memory, rescore the response after delays of 10 and 100 times the initial wait, with and without an intervening recall test. Most models keeping at least half their memories at the longest delay, and recall rarely erasing them, would confirm the claim; majority loss, or recall systematically destroying the trace, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: The initial waiting period is model-relative, so the 100-fold delay must be taken from the same definition as the code.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.75
analysis feasibility: 0.62
data existence: 0.85
data adequacy: 0.82
